The video displays grainy, black-and-white archival footage of an early biplane on a flat, open field. Initially, the aircraft is shown on the ground near a tall wooden launch structure, with several people standing nearby. As the narration states, "And so we are left with the story of the Wright brothers," the scene transitions to the plane moving along the ground and then lifting into the air. The narrator continues, "When they first flew in front of a movie camera, we have believed their version of history, that the Wright brothers flew first at Kitty Hawk in 1903." The footage follows the biplane as it gains altitude and flies low over the landscape, with a line of trees visible in the background, before the clip ends with the aircraft in flight.
ASR: And so we are left with the story of the Wright brothers. When they first flew in front of a movie camera, we have believed their version of history, that the Wright brothers flew first at Kitty Hawk in 1903.

The video opens with grainy, black-and-white archival footage from 1908 showing a group of men in early 20th-century attire, including bowler hats and long coats, walking across a flat, open field toward a distant biplane. As the narration explains that these are the first moving pictures of a Wright plane, the men continue their approach across the muddy terrain. The scene then transitions to a modern, dimly lit museum exhibit featuring a large, full-scale replica of a Wright biplane suspended from the ceiling by wooden poles. Below the aircraft, a long white display case contains documents, and the narration notes that by this time, the Wright brothers had secured a lucrative aviation patent for their control system.
ASR: to get a modified version of their biplane into the air. These first moving pictures of a Wright plane were taken in 1908. By now the Wright brothers had taken out a lucrative aviation patent for their control system.

The video displays historical black-and-white footage of early aviation experiments. Initially, a biplane is shown on the ground next to a tall wooden launch structure, with several people standing nearby. A counterweight is then seen suspended from the structure. The scene shifts to show the biplane moving across a flat, open field, gaining speed before lifting off the ground. As the aircraft ascends into the air, a group of onlookers watches from the field. The narration states that by 1905, the Wright brothers managed to get a modified version of their biplane into the air.

A black-and-white image displays a historical tablet inscribed with the text: "THE FIRST SUCCESSFUL FLIGHT OF AN AIRPLANE WAS MADE FROM THIS SPOT BY ORVILLE WRIGHT DECEMBER 17, 1903, IN A MACHINE DESIGNED AND BUILT BY WILBUR WRIGHT AND ORVILLE WRIGHT. THIS TABLET WAS ERECTED BY THE NATIONAL AERONAUTIC ASSOCIATION OF THE U.S.A. DECEMBER 17, 1926 TO COMMEMORATE THE TWENTY-FOURTH ANNIVERSARY OF THIS EVENT." As the tablet remains on screen, a narrator states that for the Wright brothers, the endeavor seemed to be less about inventing the aeroplane and more about making money.
ASR: [Brown] For the Wright brothers, it seems to have not been so much about inventing the aeroplane as about making money.

The video displays black-and-white archival footage of early aviation experiments. Initially, a large, skeletal biplane glider is shown suspended in the air against a cloudy sky, seemingly tethered by cables. The scene then transitions to a different aircraft, a powered biplane with a visible propeller at the front, flying with a pilot lying prone on the lower wing. As these images are shown, the narration explains that "they needed light-weight engines for their gliders, just like the ones invented by Whitehead."
ASR: But they needed light-weight engines for their gliders, just like the ones invented by Whitehead.

The video displays a close-up view of a newspaper article discussing early aviation experiments. The camera slowly pans across the text, which details the work of inventors Gustave Whitehead and W. D. Custead in Bridgeport, Conn. As the view moves over the paragraph describing Whitehead's "flying machine" with wings that soar like a bird, the narration states, "He has demonstrated that his machine can fly." The text on screen further clarifies that while Whitehead has shown his machine can fly, he does not claim it can be a commercial success, contrasting this with Custead's work on an airship for transportation.
ASR: "He has demonstrated that his machine can fly."

The segment opens with a view of a large, white biplane, the Wright Flyer, displayed inside a museum. As a man speaks about the price of truth and the role of museums, the camera pans across the aircraft's structure. The scene then cuts to the man standing in a hangar in front of a yellow biplane, continuing his statement. Following this, a narrator questions whether the Wright brothers or Gustave Whitehead truly kick-started the age of aviation. The video transitions to a historical reenactment showing two men in early 20th-century attire standing in a large workshop, followed by a man in a bowler hat working on an aircraft outdoors. The segment concludes with a shot of a biplane flying through a cloudy sky with the sun shining brightly.
ASR: [man] If the price of telling the truth is losing the Wright Flyer, to me, a museum tells the truth. [narrator] The Wright brothers or Gustave Whitehead? Who really kick-started the age of aviation?

The video displays black-and-white archival footage of the Wright brothers' 1903 flyer on a flat, sandy terrain. Initially, a side view shows a pilot lying prone on the lower wing structure near the center of the aircraft. The scene then transitions to a wider side profile of the biplane, highlighting its long wingspan and dual propellers, with a figure standing in the distance to the right. Finally, the camera presents a direct head-on view of the aircraft, clearly revealing the horizontally mounted engine and the low-lying pilot position. As these close-ups are shown, the narration explains that the design features a horizontally mounted engine and a low-lying pilot, noting that the aircraft would not resemble three blobs when viewed from a distance.
ASR: Close-ups of the Wright brothers' 1903 flyer show a horizontally mounted engine and a low-lying pilot, nothing that would look like three blobs from a distance.

The man in the center, wearing a blue jacket, gestures as he speaks, explaining that they are teaming up with local historian John Tchaikovsky to visit the site. He indicates that the location ahead is where Gustave would have taken off, specifically Magee-Women's Hospital, noting that it is where he was born. There's now solid evidence that not the Wright brothers but Gustave Whitehead was the first person to fly a powered aeroplane.

The video depicts the Wright brothers' early aviation experiments on the sandy dunes of Kitty Hawk. Initially, two men in dark suits are shown standing on the sand as a white, unpowered glider hovers above them. The scene transitions to show the glider resting on the ground with a person lying prone on its lower wing, followed by black-and-white archival footage of men holding the glider steady and then launching it into the air from a dune. The narration explains that after two years of experimenting with these unpowered gliders, an engine was attached to one of their flyers. The year "1903" appears on screen over a colorized image of the powered aircraft. The segment concludes with a close-up of the plane's structure and a shot of feet running on the sand, as the narration notes that the first attempt on December 14, 1903, ended in a crash.
ASR: At the same time, 600 kilometers south of Bridgeport, the Wright brothers were still experimenting with unpowered gliders, harnessing the strong coastal winds of Kitty Hawk for their glides. After two years of experimenting, an engine was attached to one of their flyers. A first attempt, on the 14th of December 1903, ended in a crash.
